questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked
This question demonstrates end-to-end supply chain security expertise: image signing, SBOM provenance tracking, CVE scanning, and runtime verification in a multi-cloud, high-stakes environment. It tests knowledge of Sigstore ecosystem tools and policy enforcement.

- Image signing with Cosign/Sigstore for supply chain integrity
- CycloneDX SBOM generation for component transparency
- CVE scanning integration (e.g., Trivy, Snyk) for vulnerability detection
- Gatekeeper/OPA policy for runtime enforcement
- Canary deployments and rollback strategies in multi-cloud contexts

## Code Example

### GitHub Actions Workflow (`.github/workflows/ci.yaml`)
```yaml
name: Image Provenance Gate
on: [push, pull_request]

jobs:
  build-scan-sign:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      
      - name: Build and push image
        run: |
          docker build -t ghcr.io/org/app:${{ github.sha }} .
          docker push ghcr.io/org/app:${{ github.sha }}
      
      - name: Generate CycloneDX SBOM
        uses: cyclonedx/ghcr-create-sbom@v1
        with:
          format: json
          output-file: sbom.json
      
      - name: Run CVE scan
        uses: aquasecurity/trivy-action@master
        with:
          image-ref: 'ghcr.io/org/app:${{ github.sha }}'
          format: json
          exit-code: '1'
          severity: 'CRITICAL,HIGH'
      
      - name: Sign image with Cosign
        uses: sigstore/cosign-installer@v3
        with:
          cosign-version: 'v2'
      - name: Sign image
        run: |
          cosign sign --yes ghcr.io/org/app:${{ github.sha }}
      
      - name: Generate SBOM with Syft
        run: |
          syft ghcr.io/org/app:${{ github.sha }} -o cyclonedx-json > sbom.json
```

### Gatekeeper Policy (`constraint-template.yaml`)
```yaml
apiVersion: templates.gatekeeper.sh/v1
kind: ConstraintTemplate
metadata:
  name: requirecosignsignature
spec:
  crd:
    spec:
      names:
        kind: RequireCosignSignature
      targets:
        - target: admission.k8s.gatekeeper.sh
          rego: |
            package requirecosignsignature
            violation["image is not signed with Cosign"] {
              image := input.review.object.spec.containers[_].image
              notcosign.verify(image)
            }
```

### Failing Manifest (Unsigned Image)
```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: unsigned-app
spec:
  containers:
  - name: app
    image: ghcr.io/org/app:unsigned-latest
    ports:
    - containerPort: 8080
```

### Passing Manifest (Signed Image)
```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: signed-app
spec:
  containers:
  - name: app
    image: ghcr.io/org/app:v1.0.0
    ports:
    - containerPort: 8080
```

### Verification Steps
```bash
# Verify image signature
cosign verify ghcr.io/org/app:v1.0.0

# Verify SBOM exists
cosign verify-attestation --type cyclonedx ghcr.io/org/app:v1.0.0

# Verify against Gatekeeper policy
kubectl get requirecosignsignature
```

## Why This Is Asked

Tests ability to implement real-world security gates that combine image scanning, attestation, and policy enforcement in a scalable multi‑tenant environment.

## Key Concepts

- Admission control with OPA/Kyverno
- SBOMs and CVE scoring via Trivy
- Image signing with cosign and Rekor attestation
- PR‑level gating and local verification

## Code Example

```yaml
# GitHub Actions: scan SBOM, sign, and publish attestation
name: Security Gate
on: [pull_request]
steps:
  - uses: actions/checkout@v4
  - name: Run Trivy SBOM
    run: trivy image --format cyclonedx -o sbom.json image:tag
  - name: Cosign sign SBOM
    run: cosign sign -key cosign.pub sbom.json
  - name: Rekor attestation
    run: cosign attest sbom.json --type sbom --format json
```

```yaml
# OPA policy (partial) enforcing CVE threshold and SBOM signing
package gate
default allow = false
allow {
  input.images[_].cve_score <= 6.0
  input.images[_].sbom_signed
}
```

```yaml

kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: example-fail
spec:
  template:
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: app
        image: registry.example/unsafe:latest
        imagePullPolicy: IfNotPresent

# passing: compliant image
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: example-pass
spec:
  template:
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: app
        image: registry.example/secure:1.0.0
        imagePullPolicy: IfNotPresent
```

## Why This Is Asked
Real-world multi-tenant data platforms require strong admission control to enforce image provenance and host security postures across clouds. Gatekeeper with Rego enables centralized policy with testable manifests.

## Key Concepts
- Open Policy Agent Gatekeeper
- ConstraintTemplate and Constraint objects
- Image provenance: registry, non-latest, digest
- Pod hardening: resources, securityContext, privilegeEscalation
- Namespace labeling and admission scope
- CI validation: conftest, gatekeeper audit, sample manifests

## Code Example
```yaml
# ConstraintTemplate (ImageProvenanceAndSecurity)
apiVersion: templates.gatekeeper.sh/v1
kind: ConstraintTemplate
metadata:
  name: imageprovenance
spec:
  crd:
    spec:
      names:
        kind: ImageProvenanceConstraint
  targets:
    - target: admission.k8s.gatekeeper.sh
      rego: |
        package imageprovenance
        violation[{"msg": msg}] {
          some i
          container := input.review.object.spec.template.spec.containers[i]
          image := container.image
          startswith(image, "registry.example.com/")
          not endswith(image, ":latest")
          some digest := input.review.object.spec.template.spec.containers[i].imageDigest
          msg := "image must be from registry.example.com with digest"
        }
```
```yaml
# Constraint (ImageProvenanceConstraint)
apiVersion: constraints.gatekeeper.sh/v1beta1
kind: ImageProvenanceConstraint
metadata:
  name: require-provenance
spec:
  enforcementAction: deny
```

```yaml
# Failing manifest: unsigned or latest, missing resources
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: data-processor
  namespace: data
spec:
  replicas: 1
  template:
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: proc
        image: registry.example.com/data/processor:latest
        imagePullPolicy: IfNotPresent
```

```yaml
# Passing manifest: compliant image, resources, and securityContext
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: data-processor
  namespace: data
spec:
  replicas: 1
  template:
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: proc
        image: registry.example.com/data/processor@sha256:abcdef...
        resources:
          requests:
            cpu: "100m"
            memory: "128Mi"
          limits:
            cpu: "500m"
            memory: "512Mi"
        securityContext:
          runAsNonRoot: true
          allowPrivilegeEscalation: false
          readOnlyRootFilesystem: true
```

## Follow-up Questions
- How would you test policy changes locally before applying to cluster?
- How would you roll out a breaking policy change across multiple namespaces without downtime?

- Pinning base images (tags or digests, not latest)

- Minimizing RUN layers via chained commands and restricted apt usage

## Code Example

```python
#!/usr/bin/env python3
import glob,os,re
for f in glob.glob('**/Dockerfile', recursive=True):
  s=open(f).read()
  if 'USER 0' in s or 'USER root' in s:
    print(f+': non-root USER not set')
  if re.search(r'FROM\s+.*:latest', s, re.M):
    print(f+': base image pinned is missing')
  if 'HEALTHCHECK' not in s:
    print(f+': HEALTHCHECK missing')
```

## Why This Is Asked
This checks namespace discipline and registry trust in manifests, a common pitfall in multi-environment apps.

## Key Concepts
- YAML manifest parsing (basic PyYAML)
- Simple allowlists for namespaces and image registries
- Tag validation (reject :latest)
- CI gate integration (GitHub Actions)

## Code Example
```python
# manifestlint.py
import yaml, sys
ALLOWED_NS = {"dev","staging","prod"}
ALLOWED_REG = {"registry.trusted"}

def ok(manifest):
  docs = yaml.safe_load_all(manifest)
  for m in docs or []:
    if m.get("kind") in {"Deployment","StatefulSet","DaemonSet"}:
      ns = m.get("metadata", {}).get("namespace")
      if ns not in ALLOWED_NS:
        return False
      for c in m.get("spec", {}).get("template", {}).get("spec", {}).get("containers", []):
        img = c.get("image", "")
        if not any(img.startswith(r) for r in ALLOWED_REG) or ":latest" in img:
          return False
  return True

if __name__ == '__main__':
  path = sys.argv[1]
  with open(path) as f:
    print(ok(f.read()))
```

## Follow-up Questions
- How would you adapt for Helm templating?  
- How would you run this as a pre-commit hook?

questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked
This question tests end-to-end security design for multi-cloud Kubernetes workloads, focusing on identity, secret management, and policy enforcement with real-world tools.

## Key Concepts
- Zero-trust workload identity (SPIRE)
- Ephemeral credentials (Vault)
- Service mesh security (Istio, mTLS, AuthorizationPolicies)
- Policy-as-code (OPA/Rego)
- Egress controls to data lake and namespace isolation

## Sample Solution

### 1. SPIRE Workload Identity
```yaml
# spire-workload.yaml
apiVersion: spire.spiffe.io/v1alpha1
kind: ClusterSPIFFEID
metadata:
  name: data-platform-workload
spec:
  names:
    - data-service
    - analytics-service
    - etl-service
  namespaceSelector:
    matchLabels:
      environment: production
```

### 2. Vault Integration for Secrets
```yaml
# vault-secret-store.yaml
apiVersion: secrets.hashicorp.com/v1beta1
kind: VaultSecret
metadata:
  name: data-lake-credentials
  namespace: data-platform
spec:
  vaultAddress: https://vault.data-platform.svc.cluster.local:8200
  path: secret/data-lake
  provider: hcp
  refreshInterval: 1h
```

### 3. Istio AuthorizationPolicy
```yaml
# istio-authz.yaml
apiVersion: security.istio.io/v1beta1
kind: AuthorizationPolicy
metadata:
  name: data-lake-access
  namespace: data-platform
spec:
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: data-lake-gateway
  rules:
  - from:
    - source:
        principals: ["spiffe://data-platform/data-service"]
    to:
    - operation:
        methods: ["GET", "POST"]
        paths: ["/v1/tables/*"]
```

### 4. OPA Policy Example
```rego
#.rego
package kubernetes.admission

deny[msg] {
  input.request.kind.kind == "Pod"
  input.request.namespace == "restricted"
  not input.request.object.spec.securityContext.runAsNonRoot
  msg = "Pods must run as non-root"
}

allow[msg] {
  input.request.kind.kind == "Deployment"
  input.request.object.spec.template.spec.containers[_].securityContext.privileged
  msg = "Privileged containers not allowed"
}
```

### 5. CI Enforcement Check
```yaml
# .github/workflows/security-scan.yml
name: Security Scan
on: [push, pull_request]
jobs:
  opa-check:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - name: Run OPA policy check
        run: |
          opa eval --fail-defined-deny \
            --data policy.rego \
            --input manifests/
```

## Key Takeaways
- SPIRE provides cryptographically secure workload identity
- Vault enables dynamic secret rotation without application changes
- Istio mTLS ensures service-to-service encryption
- OPA/Rego enforces admission control and runtime policies

## Why This Is Asked

This question evaluates practical understanding of Kubernetes security primitives including RBAC, ServiceAccount isolation, PodSecurityContext, and admission controls—essential skills for securing containerized workloads.

## Key Concepts

- **Namespace-scoped RBAC**: Role and RoleBinding for resource access control within specific namespaces
- **ServiceAccount isolation**: Dedicated service accounts to separate pod identities and permissions
- **PodSecurityContext**: Security constraints including runAsNonRoot, runAsUser, readOnlyRootFilesystem, and capability dropping
- **Admission controls**: PodSecurity standards and OPA Gatekeeper for policy enforcement at admission time

## Code Example

```yaml
# ServiceAccount (dev)
apiVersion: v1
kind: ServiceAccount
metadata:
  name: data-processor-sa
  namespace: dev
---
# Role for read-only access to ConfigMaps and Secrets
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: Role
metadata:
  name: data-processor-role
  namespace: dev
rules:
- apiGroups: [""]
  resources: ["configmaps", "secrets"]
  verbs: ["get", "list"]
---
# RoleBinding
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: RoleBinding
metadata:
  name: data-processor-binding
  namespace: dev
subjects:
- kind: ServiceAccount
  name: data-processor-sa
  namespace: dev
roleRef:
  kind: Role
  name: data-processor-role
  apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io
```

## Follow-up Questions

- How would you test the RBAC permissions locally?
- What changes are needed for the prod namespace?
- How would you implement network policies alongside these security controls?

## Why This Is Asked
Tests hands-on signing, attestation generation, and runtime enforcement across data-plane components (Airflow, Spark, Kubernetes). It probes operational trade-offs like key rotation and attestation storage.

## Key Concepts
- cosign attestations and SBOMs
- private artifact registries
- runtime policy (Kyverno/OPA)
- data-plane integration (Airflow, SparkSubmit)

## Code Example

```javascript
// Example sequence:
cosign generate-key-pair
cosign sign --key cosign.key registry.example.org/pipeline/transforms.jar:sha256:<digest>
cosign attest --predicate sbom.json --key cosign.key registry.example.org/pipeline/transforms.jar:sha256:<digest>
```

## Follow-up Questions
- How would you rotate keys without breaking existing attestations?
- How would you test the end-to-end policy in CI/CD?

questions.explanation:
This question evaluates end-to-end security across CI, admission control, and runtime enforcement in a multi-cloud, multi-tenant Kubernetes environment. It assesses understanding of image provenance, SBOM handling, and runtime integrity enforcement.

Key concepts tested include:
- Sigstore Cosign attestations and keyless verification workflows
- SBOM generation with Syft and SPDX/CycloneDX formats
- Digest pinning to prevent tag-based supply chain attacks
- OPA/Kyverno policy engine configuration and validation patterns
- Kubernetes security contexts (readOnlyRootFilesystem, runAsNonRoot, seccompProfile)
- Pod Security Standards and namespace-level enforcement
- Multi-tenant isolation and least-privilege container execution
